The Masterclass Core Thesis: Traditional SE vs. Harness Engineering
Deterministic IT Engineering ➔ Non-Deterministic Agentic AI Control Systems

• Traditional Software Engineering: Built for deterministic IT systems using frameworks (SDLC, Agile, DevOps, CI/CD, architecture patterns, testing pyramids, SRE, secure-SDLC/AppSec) to encode explicit logic with repeatable outputs for identical inputs.

• Harness Engineering: The corresponding engineering discipline for non-deterministic agentic AI systems, where runtime behavior emerges probabilistically from a model plus prompts, dynamic context, memory, tools, execution loops, policies, evaluations, and multi-agent orchestration.

• The Core Role of the Harness: Engineers the deterministic control environment surrounding the model so agentic AI systems become reliable, observable, secure, governable, and operationally manageable.

• Deterministic Control Layer: Memory (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) · Path Sandboxing (Path.is_relative_to()) · Hooks (PreToolUse/PostToolUse) · Test Feedback (Pytest TDA) · Permission Gateways (approvals.json).

MODULE 1: Why Harness Engineering
Probabilistic Model vs. Deterministic Control System
• Model Capability ≠ production reliability: Fast generation, weak follow-through without harness controls.
• Probabilistic Model Layer: Proposes code; prone to amnesia, hallucination, drift, and retry traps.
• Deterministic Harness Layer: Enforces sandboxing, AST parsing, loop detection, and secret scanning.
• Key Failure Modes: Context decay, repetitive execution loops, destructive shell commands, unverified edits.
• Core Mandate: The harness, not the model, is the control system — optimize for trust over raw speed.
Universal Environment Setup (Run Once)
Interactive Terminal Setup for All 10 Module Labs
• First time here? Set up once, then every module lab runs the same way:
• Step 1 - Clone it (not a ZIP: module 8 drives git worktree and needs .git): git clone https://github.com/kenhuangus/packt-harness.git
• Step 2 - Enter directory & create venv: cd packt-harness then python -m venv .venv
• Step 3 - Install: .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e .   (macOS/Linux: .venv/bin/python -m pip install -e .)
• Step 4 - Check it: python run_all_modules.py   expects Summary: 14 passed, 0 failed
• Why the venv: each module launches pytest with sys.executable, so the interpreter that starts a module is the one that runs its tests - it cannot pass by finding another Python on PATH

Pillar 1: Memory Files & Auto Memory in Claude Code
How Claude Remembers Your Project: CLAUDE.md Files vs. Auto Memory

• Dual Memory Architecture: Each Claude Code session begins with a fresh context window. Knowledge carries over via two complementary systems: CLAUDE.md files (instructions you write) and Auto Memory (notes Claude writes automatically).
• CLAUDE.md vs. Auto Memory Comparison:
• CLAUDE.md Files: Written by you; holds instructions, coding standards & architecture; scoped to project/user/managed policy; loaded in full at session start.
• Auto Memory (~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/): Written by Claude; holds build commands, debugging insights & discovered preferences; loaded first 200 lines / 25KB of MEMORY.md.

• Live Student Demo (MEMORY.md): [C:\Users\kenhu\.claude\projects\C--Users-kenhu-security-tools\memory\MEMORY.md](file:///C:/Users/kenhu/.claude/projects/C--Users-kenhu-security-tools/memory/MEMORY.md) (Real-world auto memory index & topic notes created by Claude Code).
• Multi-Tier Scope Precedence (Broadest to Most Specific):
• 1. Managed Policy: Organization-wide IT policy (/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md or C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md).
• 2. User Instructions: Personal preferences across all projects (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md).
• 3. Project Instructions: Shared repository standards (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md).
• 4. Local Instructions: Personal project-specific preferences; gitignored (./CLAUDE.local.md).
• 5. Path-Scoped Rules: Modular rules in .claude/rules/*.md scoped by glob patterns (paths: ['src/api/**/*.ts']).
• AGENTS.md Interoperability: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, so add @AGENTS.md into CLAUDE.md or symlink ln -s AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md for cross-agent compatibility.

• Compaction Survival & Enforcement Boundary: Root CLAUDE.md survives /compact and re-injects automatically into context. Memory files guide behavior; use PreToolUse hooks for non-negotiable security blocks.

• Live Example Link (MEMORY.md): [C:\Users\kenhu\.claude\projects\C--Users-kenhu-security-tools\memory\MEMORY.md](file:///C:/Users/kenhu/.claude/projects/C--Users-kenhu-security-tools/memory/MEMORY.md)
• Official Documentation Index: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt (Guide: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory)
• Advanced Research & Benchmarks: https://kenhuangus.github.io/agent-memory-harness/presentation/#1

Pillar 3: Hooks & The 31-Event Lifecycle Map in Claude Code
Deterministic Guardrails Across 6 Interception Categories

• 31 Lifecycle Hooks: Claude Code provides 31 deterministic PascalCase lifecycle events configured in .claude/settings.json, giving exact programmatic control over every agent turn, shell command, worktree, and memory compaction.
• 1. Session & Turn (7 hooks): SessionStart, Setup (CI/script flags), UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, Stop, StopFailure, SessionEnd (manages environment initialization & turn teardown).

• 2. Tool & Execution Loop (6 hooks): PreToolUse (security blocker; exit code 2 blocks execution), PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, PostToolUse (AST parsing & secret filtering), PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch.
• 3. Subagent & Team Orchestration (5 hooks): SubagentStart, SubagentStop (quality gates), TeammateIdle, TaskCreated, TaskCompleted (enforces 'Definition of Done' checks before accepting work).

• 4. Environment, Config & Worktrees (7 hooks): InstructionsLoaded (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md), ConfigChange, CwdChanged, DirectoryAdded, FileChanged, WorktreeCreate, WorktreeRemove (ephemeral git worktree isolation).
• 5. Context Compaction (2 hooks): PreCompact (intercepts token pressure), PostCompact (re-injects critical project rules after memory compression).
• 6. MCP & System Interaction (4 hooks): Notification (Slack/desktop alerts), MessageDisplay, Elicitation, ElicitationResult (sanitizes user response before sending to MCP servers).
Pillars 4 & 5: Budget & Tracing (Claude Code JSONL Transcripts)
Context Allocation & Immutable Audit Logs (~/.claude/projects/<encoded-path>/<session-id>.jsonl)
• Pillar 4: Context Token Budgeting & Compaction (ContextTokenBudgeter in core_harness_stack.py):
• 20/20/50/10 Token Allocation: 20% Memory (CLAUDE.md), 20% Spec (SPEC.md), 50% Workspace (active code/diffs), 10% Output Headroom.
• Head/Tail Compaction: Preserves first 5 & last 15 lines/turns of conversation history, omitting noisy intermediate logs to prevent context drift.
• Pillar 5: Structured Tracing & Claude Code JSONL Transcript Architecture:
• File Layout & Storage: Stored under ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-project-path>/<session-id>.jsonl (one file per session UUID, append-only, one JSON object per line).
• Common Top-Level Schema: type (user/assistant/system), uuid, parentUuid, timestamp (ISO 8601), sessionId, cwd, gitBranch, and version.
• Event Types & Payloads: type: 'user' (prompts & tool_result blocks), type: 'assistant' (text, thinking, tool_use blocks, and message.usage token accounting).
• Direct Audit Inspection (jq/Python): Scan tool calls via jq -c 'select(.type=="assistant") | .message.content[] | select(.type=="tool_use") | {name, input}' or query token usage via .message.usage.
• Lab demo: https://github.com/kenhuangus/packt-harness/blob/main/course_implementation/module_02_core_harness_stack/README.md

MODULE 3: Spec-Driven Development
Why Prompts Fail & Machine-Readable Specs Succeed
• Prompts are ambiguous, under-specified, and prone to context drift over long chats.
• Machine-Verifiable Contracts: SPEC.md defines allowed file scopes, schemas, and non-goals.
• Hard Scope Boundaries: SpecVerifier rejects out-of-scope diffs and blocks unapproved writes.
• Non-Goal Filtering: Blocks architectural sprawl and unrequested dependencies before code is saved.
• Automated Verification: Verifies syntax via ast.parse() and runs pytest before shipping.
SPEC.md Anatomy
Required Sections
• 1. Objective & Scope (allowed/forbidden files)
• 2. Explicit Non-Goals (no DB pool, no OAuth2)
• 3. Input/Output Schemas (token -> dict)
• 4. Acceptance Criteria (AC-01 through AC-04)
Scope and Non-Goals
Hard Boundaries
• Allowed Files: auth_validator.py, test_auth.py
• Forbidden Files: database.py, config/settings.py
• Non-Goal: Rejects connect_db & OAuth2 rotation
• Sandboxing: Bound via Path.is_relative_to()
Acceptance Criteria
Machine-Verifiable Contracts
• AC-01: Exports validate_jwt(token: str) -> dict
• AC-02: Returns valid=True, user_id=123 for live JWT
• AC-03: Returns valid=False, error=EXPIRED for expired JWT
• AC-04: Passes all automated tests in test_auth.py

MODULE 6: Tests as Reliability Layer
The Test-Driven Coding Agent (TDCA)
• Grounded Execution: Replace unverified agent claims with deterministic pytest subprocess return codes.
• Real Traceback Capture: Feed raw stdout/stderr error tracebacks directly into repair prompts without copy-paste.
• Anti-Regression Safeguards: Automatically register discovered bugs as permanent test suite fixtures.
• Quantitative Reliability: Track first-pass pass rate, mean repair iterations, and regression count.
Test Tiers for Agentic AI Systems
Comprehensive Verification Pyramid: From Unit Testing to Red Teaming
• 1. Unit Testing: Isolates individual functions, schema serializers, and tool validators.
• 2. Integration Testing: Verifies component boundaries, tool invocations, and MCP protocol handshakes.
• 3. End-to-End (E2E) Testing: Executes complete multi-turn workflows from initial user prompt to finished artifact.
• 4. Regression Testing: Captures every historical failure and automatically appends it to the test suite fixture.
• 5. Performance & Scalability Testing: Benchmarks agent concurrency, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), and token throughput under load.
• 6. Full UI Testing: Validates end-to-end visual flows, DOM interactions, and human-in-the-loop frontend review screens.
• 7. Security Testing & Red Teaming: Pen-testing for prompt injection, jailbreaks, SSRF, credential extraction, and unauthorized tool escalation.
Pytest Capture vs. Observability Platforms
Dual-Loop Architecture: Black-Box Verification & Glass-Box Tracing

• Local vs. Distributed Observability: Pytest Capture (capfd) is a local test runner ('Black Box' Outer Loop), while Langfuse, LangSmith, and Arize are distributed observability platforms ('Glass Box / X-Ray' Inner Loop).
| Feature | Pytest Capture (capfd) | Langfuse / LangSmith / Arize | OpenAI SDK Tracing |
| Primary Role | Test Runner & Output Verifier | LLM Observability & Debugging | Raw API Logging |
| What it Captures | Local stdout / stderr & exit codes | Full trace of prompts, tool calls, costs | Raw HTTP request / response payloads |
| Visibility | Black Box (Final artifacts & side effects) | Glass Box (Internal reasoning & retries) | Network Level (Payloads only) |
| Best Use Case | CI/CD Pass/Fail: Customer Acceptance | Root-Cause Debugging & Cost Tracking | Low-level connection debugging |
• The Dual-Loop Pattern in Production:
• Outer Loop (Pytest): Asserts final deliverables — Did the agent create valid files? Did tests exit 0? Did stderr stay clean?
• Inner Loop (LangSmith / Langfuse): Diagnoses execution path — Why 3 retries? Did it hallucinate tools? What was the token cost?
• Best Practice: Start with zero-setup Pytest Capture for deterministic correctness; add Langfuse/LangSmith later to optimize costs and reasoning.
Anti-Regression
Keep the Bug
• Every failure becomes a test
• Append it to the suite
• Rerun before you ship
• Lab demo: https://github.com/kenhuangus/packt-harness/blob/main/course_implementation/module_06_tests_as_reliability_layer/README.md
Evaluation Harnesses for Agentic AI
The Hardest Frontier in AI Engineering

• The Hardest Engineering Challenge: Evaluating autonomous agents (especially coding agents) is notoriously difficult due to non-deterministic multi-turn trajectories, dynamic state explosion, and test contamination.
• Strict Evaluation Isolation: the evaluator must run in an external, independent control sandbox completely out of the agent's context and reach.
• Industry Benchmark Examples:
• SWE-bench (Verified / Lite): Real-world GitHub issues evaluated against hidden unit test assertions.
• HumanEval & MBPP: Function-level code synthesis and unit-test benchmarks.
• TerminalBench & InterCode: Multi-turn interactive bash shell and CLI execution tasks.
• In-Repo Deterministic Replay Suites: Scored on test pass rate, scope fidelity, token spend, and permission denies.

MODULE 7: Agent Extensions with Skills, Plugins, MCP etc.
Extending Agent Capabilities via SOPs, Tool Servers & Distribution Bundles
• Modular Architecture: Decouples domain knowledge (Skills), executable tool servers (MCP), and distribution packages (Plugins).
• Skills (SKILL.md): Standardized Markdown SOPs loaded on demand via progressive disclosure.
• Plugins (.claude-plugin/plugin.json): Self-contained bundles packaging skills, hooks, MCP servers, and subagents.
• Model Context Protocol (MCP): Open standard exposing deterministic tools (@mcp.tool) and resources over stdio and Streamable HTTP.
Agent Skills & Directory Layout
Standard Architecture: SKILL.md, Scripts & References
• Self-Contained Modularity: Encapsulates domain expertise, execution scripts, and API schemas in one directory.
• SKILL.md Entry Point: YAML frontmatter with description defining what the skill does and when to use it.
• Progressive Disclosure: Heavy scripts/ and references/ are only loaded into context when triggered.
• Precedence Hierarchy (Highest to Lowest): 1. Enterprise Managed > 2. Personal User-Level (~/.claude/skills/) > 3. Project Root (.claude/skills/).

• OWASP Agentic Skill Top 10 Risks: https://owasp.org/www-project-agentic-skills-top-10/ (Standardized security taxonomy covering prompt injection in instructions, malicious tool schemas, unauthorized data egress, and unvalidated script execution in agent skills).
• Video Walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l-uwnCzRRE0 (In-depth breakdown of OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 risks & defenses).
Plugin Architecture: plugin.json vs. marketplace.json
Local Implementation Blueprint vs. Global Distribution Registry

• plugin.json (Internal Blueprint): Resides locally at .claude-plugin/plugin.json. Maps plugin identity (e.g., "name": "db-helper", "version": "1.0.0"), execution boundaries, language runtimes, companion agents, hooks, and MCP servers so the Claude client can register and isolate that specific tool on your machine.

• marketplace.json (Public Registry): Operates as the ecosystem distribution catalog. Acts as an index pointing to secure hosting locations, verified developer profiles, version histories, and download URLs (e.g., listing db-helper with author & compatibility requirements) so users can safely discover and install plugins.

• Strict Operational Hierarchy: While plugin.json configures how a single tool functions under the hood locally, marketplace.json manages how users discover, download, and safely install that tool from an approved repository or enterprise store.
Model Context Protocol (MCP): Architecture & Protocol Evolution
Host, Client, Server, Tools & Modern Stateless JSON-RPC 2.0
• 4 Core MCP Architecture Roles:
• MCP Host: Overarching runtime environment (Claude Code, Cursor) managing the chat session & coordinating external endpoints without application bloat.
• MCP Client: Nested 1-to-1 connection manager handling feature discovery, authentication, intent-to-call translation, and output formatting.
• MCP Server: Independent service abstracting databases (Postgres), APIs (GitHub), or filesystems locally or remotely.
• MCP Tools, Resources & Prompts: Actionable capabilities (@mcp.tool decorators with JSON Schema), raw readable data URIs, and reusable prompt templates.
• Protocol Architecture & Evolution (Stateless JSON-RPC 2.0):
• Fully Stateless Requests: Protocol shifted from legacy stateful sessions to a stateless request-response model using JSON-RPC 2.0 (initialization handshake and sticky session routing removed).
• Universal Serverless Scaling: Self-contained requests allow servers to scale behind standard load balancers on AWS Lambda or Cloudflare Workers.
• Multi-Round Trip Requests (MRTR): Human input or extra authorization returns resultType: "input_required", allowing client retries to land on any server instance seamlessly.
• Flexible Transports: stdio for low-overhead local plugins; standardized HTTP/HTTPS for remote cloud infrastructure.
Securing the Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server
Threat Modeling, 3-Zone Architecture & Production Hardening Checklist
• Reference: Ken Huang — "Securing the Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server" (https://kenhuangus.substack.com/p/securing-the-model-context-protocol)
• 3-Zone Defense-in-Depth Architecture:
• Zone 0 (Control Plane): Vault dynamic secrets (PKI, 5-min TTL), Policy-as-Code engine (OPA/Cedar), and OTEL SIEM audit bus.
• Zone 1 (MCP Server Fleet): Stateless pods behind mTLS mesh, read-only rootfs, no service account automount, and sidecar OPA authz.
• Zone 2 (Tool Runtime): Firecracker micro-VMs / gVisor sandboxes per tool invocation, strict FQDN egress allowlists, and dropped capabilities (drop=ALL).
• Zone 3 (Downstream APIs): Scoped, audience-restricted tokens for SaaS, databases, and Kubernetes clusters.
• 9-Point MCP Hardening Checklist:
• 1. Transport & Auth: TLS 1.3 AES-256-GCM, mTLS with SPIFFE IDs or DPoP-bound JWTs (audience-locked to prevent cross-audience replay).
• 2. Authorization (Policy-as-Code): Default-deny OPA/Cedar evaluating subject, action, resource, and context (no wildcard tools.*).
• 3. Strict Input Validation: JSON Schema strict mode (no additionalProperties), max string length 8 kB, array length 1,000, max depth 15.
• 4. Output Sanitization & Secret Stripping: Streaming regex filter strips AWS keys (AKIA), OpenAI keys, GCP tokens, and PANs before LLM context re-entry.
• 5. Secrets Lifecycle: Dynamic Vault leases (15-min DB roles, 60-min AWS STS); never inject static root credentials into tool containers.
• 6. Sandboxed Execution: Micro-VMs (gVisor/Firecracker), readOnlyRootFilesystem=true, seccomp=RuntimeDefault, 50% RAM tmpfs scratch.
• 7. Rate Limiting & Denial-of-Wallet Guards: Token buckets (100 req/min), declared $maxCost USD quotas per tool, global circuit-breakers.
• 8. Supply-Chain Security: Pin and hash dependencies (--hash=sha256:), private PyPI mirror, Sigstore Cosign image signing & SBOM.
• 9. Human-in-the-Loop Gateways: Destructive or high-cost actions (> $50 or DROP/DELETE) require step-up FIDO2 / mobile MFA approval.
• Insecure MCP Demo: https://github.com/kenhuangus/mcp-vulnerable-server-demo (Hands-on exploration of prompt injection, SSRF & command execution vulnerabilities in MCP servers)
Comparing Agent Extension Mechanisms: MCP vs. CLI vs. Skill vs. Plugin vs. Hook
Taxonomy, Simple Definitions & Operational Boundaries
| Concept | Simple Definition | Who or What Uses It? |
| MCP | A universal bridge connecting AI models to data and tools. | AI Models |
| CLI | A text-based interface to run commands on a computer. | Humans or Scripts |
| Skill | A pre-packaged set of instructions that teaches an AI a new capability. | AI Platforms |
| Plug-in | An add-on that adds a specific feature to a software program. | Host Applications |
| Hook | A code trigger that automatically runs when a specific event happens. | Software Runtimes |
• MCP vs. CLI: MCP provides structured, typed JSON-RPC schema calls directly to AI models; CLI provides text-based command execution for developers and automation scripts.
• Skill vs. Plugin: Skills package in-context procedural knowledge and domain scripts (SKILL.md); Plugins package tools, configurations, and skills into installable add-ons (plugin.json).
• Hook vs. Tool: Tools are actively called by the AI to mutate state; Hooks are deterministic event triggers executed automatically by the runtime to enforce safety guardrails.
Multi-Agent Design Patterns & Production Hardening Framework
The 7 Core Architectural Topologies, Execution Flows & Production Hardening Checklist
• The 7 Production Multi-Agent Topologies (Ordered from Simplest to Most Complex):
• 1. Orchestrator–Worker: Central controller decomposes incoming tasks and dynamically delegates to specialized worker agents (search, code, write) with fallback routing.
• 2. Pipeline (Sequential Chain): Strictly ordered linear stages (Plan ➔ Research ➔ Draft ➔ Format) with stage-level auditing and checkpointing.
• 3. Fan-out / Fan-in (Map–Reduce): Dispatcher spawns N parallel workers over independent chunks; Reducer merges results with strict concurrency caps.
• 4. Critic–Refiner (Self-Improvement Loop): Generator produces output, Critic evaluates against rubric/tests, Refiner improves with a hard iteration cap (2-3 rounds).
• 5. Hierarchical (Multi-Tier): Root orchestrator delegates to domain sub-managers (engineering, ops) with per-tier timeouts and cancellation propagation.
• 6. Event-Driven (Reactive): Agents subscribe to message bus topics, reacting asynchronously with decoupled scaling, distributed tracing, and idempotent event handlers.
• 7. Sidecar + Human Escalation: Guard agent intercepts mutating actions (DB/API/files), routing high-risk operations to human reviewers.
• 4-Pillar Production Hardening Checklist (Universal Across All Patterns):
• Observability: Distributed trace spans per agent invocation, token cost attribution per request, error rate dashboards, and p50/p95/p99 latency percentiles.
• Reliability: Circuit breakers with exponential backoff, per-agent timeout budgets, idempotent write handlers, and state checkpointing.
• Security & Governance: Intent-Based Access Control (IBAC), least-privilege tool isolation, immutable audit logs with hashes, and global kill switch propagation.
• Context Management: Shared context bus / memory (avoids prompt bloating), RAG grounding in authoritative sources, and strict context window budget enforcement.

Graph Engineering vs. Dynamic Workflows in Claude Code

• Paradigm vs. Runtime: Graph Engineering is the broad architectural blueprint design paradigm for structuring AI into multi-agent networks; Dynamic Workflows is Anthropic’s native runtime JavaScript orchestration executing that design.
| Feature | Graph Engineering | Dynamic Workflows (Claude Code Native) |
| What it is | A structural philosophy for designing multi-agent workflows. | Anthropic’s native runtime orchestration feature. |
| Who builds it | Human architect using LangGraph, n8n, or custom DAGs. | Claude Code builds & writes it autonomously via prompt. |
| How it runs | Explicitly defined nodes, edges, state machines & code loops. | Background JavaScript script running outside active chat. |
| Context Window | Shared or scoped across custom orchestrators. | Heavily isolated; only final results return to chat window. |
| Reusability | Pre-baked pipelines optimized for predictable recurring jobs. | Saved to .claude/workflows/ as custom slash commands. |
• 1. Graph Engineering (The Blueprint): Maps out Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) with isolated nodes (sub-agents) and explicit edges/checkpoints to prevent infinite looping and token flooding.
• 2. Dynamic Workflows (Claude Code Runtime): Translates high-level prompts into real-time JS orchestration using a Fan-Out / Refute / Converge topology with background token isolation.
• Decision Guide: Use Dynamic Workflows for terminal repo refactors & large migrations; build Custom Engineering Graphs for strict enterprise compliance, permanent integrations & UI approval gates.

• Reference Sources: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zyKWWJJ9HvI, https://aipractitioner.substack.com/p/claude-dynamic-workflows-scaling, https://blakecrosley.com/guides/loop-engineering
